note.explanation: This chapter compares the properties and reactions of groups of elements. Down Group 1, metals lose their outer electron more easily and become more reactive. Down the halogens, atoms gain an electron less easily, so their reactivity decreases. Metals usually form positive ions, while halogens form negative ions.
examples: Potassium reacts with chlorine to form potassium chloride: 2K + Cl₂ → 2KCl.
Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.
note.checkAnswer: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it oxidises bromide ions to bromine.
note.simple: Remember the opposite trends: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group, but halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
note.checkQuestion: Which is the stronger oxidising agent, chlorine or bromine, and why?
note.title: Group Properties and Elements
steps: Identify the group of the elements in the question.
Recall the trend down that group.
Use the trend to compare the elements or predict the reaction.
For a reaction, write the balanced equation and identify any oxidising or reducing agent.
note.answer: Group 1 elements become more reactive down the group, while halogens become less reactive down the group.

mcqs.stem: Q9.1. Which halogen will have the least reactivity with alkaline earth metals?
rationales: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine because halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
Iodine is the least reactive option because it is lowest in the group.
Bromine is more reactive than iodine because it is above iodine in the group.
Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, not the least.

mcqs.stem: Q9.2. Which compound do you expect to be coloured?
rationales: KCl is an ionic salt of a Group 1 metal and is usually white or colourless.
BaCl₂ is usually a white or colourless ionic compound.
AlCl₃ is not the coloured compound in this set.
NiCl₂ is coloured because it contains a transition element.

mcqs.stem: Q9.3. In which element there exists the strongest forces of attraction between atoms?
rationales: Mg has the smallest atoms of these choices, so its metallic bonding is strongest.
Ca atoms are larger than Mg atoms, so the attraction is weaker than in Mg.
Sr atoms are larger than Ca atoms, so the attraction is weaker than in Mg.
Ba atoms are the largest of these choices, so the attraction is weakest.

mcqs.stem: Q9.4. Elements of which group are all coloured?
rationales: The Second group elements are not all coloured.
The textbook identifies the Sixth group as the group whose elements are all coloured.
The Fourth group elements are not all coloured.
The Fifth group elements are not all coloured.

mcqs.stem: Q9.5. Which halogen acid is unstable at room temperature?
rationales: HBr is more stable at room temperature than HI.
HI is thermally unstable because the H—I bond is relatively weak.
HCl is more stable because its H—Cl bond is stronger than the H—I bond.
HF has a very strong H—F bond and is not the unstable acid in this set.

mcqs.stem: Q9.6. Which oxide is the most basic oxide?
rationales: Na₂O is the most basic oxide among these choices.
Li₂O is basic, but it is less basic than Na₂O.
MgO is basic, but it is less basic than the Group 1 oxide Na₂O in this set.
CO is not a basic oxide.

mcqs.stem: Q9.7. Which group elements are the most reactive elements?
rationales: Transition metals are not the group identified here as the most reactive.
First group elements are highly reactive because they readily lose one outer electron.
Second group elements are reactive but generally less reactive than First group elements.
Third group elements are not the most reactive group in these choices.

mcqs.stem: Q9.8. The following solutions of a halogen and a sodium halide are mixed together. Which solution will turn dark because of a reaction?
rationales: Bromine cannot displace chlorine from sodium chloride because chlorine is more reactive.
Bromine cannot displace fluorine from sodium fluoride because fluorine is more reactive.
Chlorine cannot displace fluorine from sodium fluoride because fluorine is more reactive.
Chlorine displaces iodine from sodium iodide, producing iodine, which makes the solution dark.

options: X will displace iodine from it
mcqs.stem: Q9.9. X is a monoatomic gas, which statement about this is correct?
rationales: A monoatomic gas of this kind does not characteristically burn in air.
Noble gases are colourless, not coloured.
A monoatomic gas is a noble gas and is unreactive.
A noble gas does not displace iodine from a compound.

mcqs.stem: Q9.10. Which property is correct for group 1 elements?
rationales: Low catalytic activity is the correct property among these choices.
Group 1 elements generally have low, not high, densities.
Group 1 metals conduct electricity well, so their conductivity is not low.
Group 1 metals generally have low melting points, not high melting points.

written.text: Q9.1. Why does it become easier to cut an alkali metal when we move from top to bottom in a group?
written.finalAnswer: Atomic size increases and metallic bonding becomes weaker down the group, so the metals become softer and easier to cut.

rubric.why: The increasing size of the atoms explains the change down the group.
rubric.description: State that atomic size increases down the group.
rubric.how: Explain that the outer electron is farther from the nucleus as the atoms become larger.

rubric.why: The weakening attraction explains why the metal becomes easier to cut.
rubric.description: Link weaker metallic bonding with softness.
rubric.how: Conclude that the metal is softer and easier to cut.

modelAnswer: Atomic size increases down the group.
Metallic bonding becomes weaker, so the metals become softer and easier to cut.

written.text: Q9.2. Predict the reactivity of potassium towards halogens.
written.finalAnswer: Potassium is very reactive and reacts vigorously with halogens to form potassium halides.

rubric.why: The prediction about potassium's reactivity is essential.
rubric.description: State that potassium reacts vigorously.
rubric.how: Use the Group 1 reactivity trend to identify potassium as highly reactive.

rubric.why: The product shows what the reaction forms.
rubric.description: State that potassium forms a potassium halide.
rubric.how: Give the product or a suitable example reaction.

modelAnswer: Potassium is a highly reactive alkali metal.
It reacts vigorously with halogens to form potassium halides.

written.text:
Q9.3. In the following reaction, chlorine acts as an oxidising agent. Which is the reducing agent?

Cl₂(aq) + 2NaBr(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + Br₂(g)
written.finalAnswer: Sodium bromide (Br⁻ ions) is the reducing agent.

rubric.why: The correct reactant or ion must be identified.
rubric.description: Name sodium bromide or bromide ions.
rubric.how: Identify the species that is oxidised in the reaction.

rubric.why: This links the identified species to its role in the reaction.
rubric.description: Explain why it is the reducing agent.
rubric.how: State that bromide ions lose electrons and are oxidised.

modelAnswer: Bromide ions change into bromine: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
Therefore, sodium bromide (Br⁻ ions) is the reducing agent.

written.text: Q9.4. Why does iodine exist in the solid state at room temperature?
written.finalAnswer: Iodine molecules have strong intermolecular forces because of their large size and high relative molecular mass, so iodine is solid at room temperature.

rubric.why: The large iodine molecules account for stronger attractions between them.
rubric.description: Refer to iodine's large molecules or high relative molecular mass.
rubric.how: Link the size of iodine molecules to stronger intermolecular attraction.

rubric.why: The forces explain iodine's physical state.
rubric.description: State that the attractions hold iodine molecules in a solid.
rubric.how: Conclude that iodine is solid at room temperature.

modelAnswer: Iodine molecules are large and have strong intermolecular forces.
These forces hold the molecules together, so iodine is solid at room temperature.

written.text: Q9.5. How does Ni catalyse the reaction involving hydrogenation of oil?
written.finalAnswer: Nickel provides a surface on which hydrogen and oil are adsorbed, bringing them together and helping hydrogen add across the oil's unsaturated bonds.

rubric.why: The catalyst's surface is how the reactants are brought together.
rubric.description: State that hydrogen and oil are adsorbed on nickel.
rubric.how: Describe nickel as providing a surface for the reactants.

rubric.why: This states what the catalytic process does.
rubric.description: Explain that hydrogen adds to the oil's unsaturated bonds.
rubric.how: Describe the hydrogenation of the oil on the catalyst surface.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen and oil are adsorbed on the surface of nickel.
The nickel surface brings them together, allowing hydrogen to add across the unsaturated bonds in the oil.

written.text: Q9.1. Which noble gas should have the lowest boiling point and why?
written.finalAnswer: Helium has the lowest boiling point because its atoms are smallest and the forces of attraction between them are weakest.

rubric.why: The correct noble gas must be named.
rubric.description: Name helium.
rubric.how: Choose the smallest noble gas.

rubric.why: The explanation connects weak attractions with a low boiling point.
rubric.description: Explain the weak attraction between helium atoms.
rubric.how: State that little energy is needed to separate the atoms.

modelAnswer: Helium is the smallest noble gas.
The forces of attraction between its atoms are weakest, so it has the lowest boiling point.

written.text: Q9.2. Compare the reactions of alkali metals with chlorine.
written.finalAnswer: Alkali metals react with chlorine to form metal chlorides; their vigour increases down the group.

rubric.why: The products of the reactions must be identified.
rubric.description: State that chlorine forms alkali metal chlorides.
rubric.how: Give the general product or an example equation.

rubric.why: The comparison requires the trend in reaction vigour.
rubric.description: Compare the reactions down the group.
rubric.how: State that reaction vigour increases from the top to the bottom of Group 1.

modelAnswer: Alkali metals react with chlorine to form ionic metal chlorides.
The reactions become more vigorous down the group as the reactivity of the alkali metals increases.

written.text: Q9.3. Why are almost all the metals solids while non-metals generally exist as gases and solids?
written.finalAnswer: Strong metallic bonding holds metal atoms together as solids, while non-metals generally have weaker attractions between their particles and can therefore exist as gases or solids.

rubric.why: Strong bonding explains why almost all metals remain solid.
rubric.description: Explain the solid state of metals.
rubric.how: Refer to the strong forces or metallic bonds between metal atoms.

rubric.why: The different attractions explain the varied states of non-metals.
rubric.description: Explain why non-metals can be gases or solids.
rubric.how: Compare the weaker attractions between non-metal particles with metallic bonding.

modelAnswer: Strong metallic bonding holds metal atoms together, so almost all metals are solids.
Non-metals generally have weaker attractions between their particles and can exist as gases or solids.

written.text: Q9.4. Name any three elements in the periodic table which exist as liquids.
written.finalAnswer: Bromine, mercury and gallium (when slightly warmed).

rubric.why: Bromine is one of the elements that can be named.
rubric.description: Name bromine.
rubric.how: Give the element name.

rubric.why: Mercury is liquid at ordinary room temperature.
rubric.description: Name mercury.
rubric.how: Give the element name.

rubric.why: The third example has a melting point close to room temperature.
rubric.description: Name a third element that can exist as a liquid near room temperature.
rubric.how: Give gallium or caesium, noting that it becomes liquid slightly above ordinary room temperature.

modelAnswer: Bromine and mercury are liquids at ordinary room temperature.
Gallium also exists as a liquid when slightly warmed.

written.text: Q9.5. Why are transition elements different from normal elements?
written.finalAnswer: Transition elements have partially filled d-subshells and show properties such as variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic activity.

rubric.why: Their electronic structure is the underlying reason for their distinctive properties.
rubric.description: Refer to the partially filled d-subshell.
rubric.how: Identify the characteristic electronic structure of transition elements.

rubric.why: A characteristic property shows how transition elements differ.
rubric.description: Give one or more distinctive properties.
rubric.how: Name variable oxidation states, coloured compounds or catalytic activity.

modelAnswer: Transition elements have partially filled d-subshells.
They show characteristic properties such as variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic activity.

written.text: Q9.6. Compare the reactivity of chlorine and bromine as an oxidising agent.
written.finalAnswer: Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent and is more reactive than bromine; it can oxidise bromide ions to bromine.

rubric.why: The relative strength of the two oxidising agents must be stated.
rubric.description: Identify chlorine as the stronger oxidising agent.
rubric.how: Compare their positions in the halogen group and state the trend.

rubric.why: The displacement reaction supports the comparison.
rubric.description: Give the reaction showing chlorine oxidises bromide.
rubric.how: State that chlorine converts bromide ions into bromine.

modelAnswer: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine and is the stronger oxidising agent.
Chlorine oxidises bromide ions to bromine: Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.

written.text: Q9.7. Which element is the most reactive and which is the least reactive among halogens? Give two reasons to explain your answer.
written.finalAnswer: Fluorine is the most reactive and iodine is the least reactive. Fluorine atoms are smallest and attract an incoming electron most strongly; iodine atoms are largest and attract an incoming electron least strongly.

rubric.why: The most reactive halogen must be identified.
rubric.description: Name fluorine as the most reactive.
rubric.how: State the correct element.

rubric.why: The least reactive halogen must be identified.
rubric.description: Name iodine as the least reactive.
rubric.how: State the correct element.

rubric.why: Atomic size and attraction explain fluorine's high reactivity.
rubric.description: Give a reason for fluorine's high reactivity.
rubric.how: Explain that its small size means it attracts an incoming electron strongly.

rubric.why: The second reason explains iodine's low reactivity.
rubric.description: Give a reason for iodine's low reactivity.
rubric.how: Explain that its large size means it attracts an incoming electron less strongly.

modelAnswer: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, while iodine is the least reactive.
Fluorine has the smallest atoms and attracts an incoming electron most strongly.
Iodine has the largest atoms and attracts an incoming electron least strongly.

written.text: Q9.1. Explain the role of catalytic converter in an automobile.
written.finalAnswer: A catalytic converter uses catalysts such as platinum, palladium and rhodium to convert harmful exhaust gases, including carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons, into less harmful gases such as carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water.

rubric.why: The answer must identify where the converter works.
rubric.description: State that the converter treats automobile exhaust.
rubric.how: Mention exhaust gases from the automobile.

rubric.why: The catalysts enable the conversion reactions.
rubric.description: Name a catalyst used in the converter.
rubric.how: Give one or more of platinum, palladium or rhodium.

rubric.why: Identifying pollutants shows what the converter removes or changes.
rubric.description: Name harmful exhaust gases.
rubric.how: Give examples such as CO, nitrogen oxides or unburnt hydrocarbons.

rubric.why: The products complete the explanation of the converter's role.
rubric.description: State that the harmful gases are converted to less harmful products.
rubric.how: Name carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water where appropriate.

modelAnswer: A catalytic converter treats the exhaust gases from an automobile.
Catalysts such as platinum, palladium and rhodium help convert harmful gases.
Carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons are changed into less harmful products.
These products include carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water.

written.text: Q9.2. Why do the chemical reactivities of alkali metals increase down the group whereas they decrease down the group in case of halogens?
written.finalAnswer: Down Group 1, the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and is lost more easily, so reactivity increases. Down the halogen group, the atoms become larger and attract an incoming electron less strongly, so reactivity decreases.

rubric.why: The Group 1 trend must be stated correctly.
rubric.description: State that alkali metal reactivity increases down the group.
rubric.how: Give the direction of the trend.

rubric.why: This explains why Group 1 elements react more readily down the group.
rubric.description: Explain the Group 1 trend using the outer electron.
rubric.how: Mention increased distance or shielding and easier electron loss.

rubric.why: The halogen trend must be stated correctly.
rubric.description: State that halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
rubric.how: Give the direction of the trend.

rubric.why: This explains why halogens become less reactive down the group.
rubric.description: Explain the halogen trend in terms of gaining an electron.
rubric.how: State that larger atoms attract an incoming electron less strongly.

modelAnswer: Down Group 1, atomic size and shielding increase, so the outer electron is lost more easily.
Therefore, the reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group.
Down the halogen group, atomic size increases and the attraction for an incoming electron becomes weaker.
Therefore, the reactivity of halogens decreases down the group.

written.text: Q9.3. Why are metals generally tough and strong whereas non-metals are neither tough nor strong?
written.finalAnswer: Metals have a strong lattice of positive ions held together by delocalised electrons, making them tough and strong. Non-metals do not have this strong metallic bonding and are generally brittle or weak.

rubric.why: The bonding in metals explains their strength.
rubric.description: Describe the strong structure in metals.
rubric.how: Refer to strong metallic bonding or a strong lattice.

rubric.why: This identifies how the metallic structure is held together.
rubric.description: Explain the nature of metallic bonding.
rubric.how: Mention positive ions and delocalised electrons.

rubric.why: The contrast with metals is needed to explain the non-metal properties.
rubric.description: State that non-metals lack strong metallic bonding.
rubric.how: Describe the weaker bonding or attractions in non-metals.

rubric.why: The conclusion links the bonding difference to the stated properties.
rubric.description: State the resulting properties of non-metals.
rubric.how: Conclude that non-metals are generally brittle, not tough or not strong.

modelAnswer: Metals have a strong lattice of positive ions held together by delocalised electrons.
This strong metallic bonding makes metals tough and strong.
Non-metals do not have this strong metallic bonding.
They are generally brittle and are neither tough nor strong.

written.text: Q9.4. Both alkali metals and halogens are very reactive elements with roles opposite to each other. Explain.
written.finalAnswer: Alkali metals lose one outer electron to form positive ions, while halogens gain one electron to form negative ions; these oppositely charged ions combine to form ionic compounds.

rubric.why: The electron loss explains the role of alkali metals.
rubric.description: State what alkali metals do with their outer electron.
rubric.how: Explain that they lose one electron.

rubric.why: The product of electron loss identifies their ionic role.
rubric.description: Name the ions formed by alkali metals.
rubric.how: State that they form positive ions.

rubric.why: The electron gain explains the opposite role of halogens.
rubric.description: State what halogens do with an electron.
rubric.how: Explain that they gain one electron.

rubric.why: The final point connects the opposite ions to their compounds.
rubric.description: State the ions formed and how they combine.
rubric.how: Conclude that negative and positive ions form ionic compounds.

modelAnswer: Alkali metals lose one outer electron and form positive ions.
Halogens gain one electron and form negative ions.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other.
They combine to form ionic compounds.

written.text: Q9.5. Why hydrogen bromide is thermally unstable as compared to hydrogen chloride?
written.finalAnswer: The H—Br bond is longer and weaker than the H—Cl bond because bromine atoms are larger than chlorine atoms, so hydrogen bromide decomposes more easily on heating.

rubric.why: The size difference is the starting point for the bond-strength explanation.
rubric.description: Compare the sizes of bromine and chlorine atoms.
rubric.how: State that bromine atoms are larger.

rubric.why: The larger atom makes the H—Br bond longer.
rubric.description: State that the H—Br bond is longer.
rubric.how: Compare the bond length with H—Cl.

rubric.why: A weaker bond is more easily broken by heat.
rubric.description: State that the H—Br bond is weaker than H—Cl.
rubric.how: Compare the strength of the two bonds.

rubric.why: The conclusion explains the relative thermal stability.
rubric.description: Link the weak bond to thermal instability.
rubric.how: State that HBr decomposes more readily on heating.

modelAnswer: Bromine atoms are larger than chlorine atoms.
The H—Br bond is longer and weaker than the H—Cl bond.
Less energy is needed to break the H—Br bond.
Therefore, hydrogen bromide is thermally less stable.

written.text: Q9.6. Compare the properties of metals and non-metals.
written.finalAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors of heat and electricity, and mostly solids with high melting points. Non-metals are generally dull, brittle when solid, poor conductors, and may be gases or solids with lower melting points.

rubric.why: Appearance is one clear comparison between metals and non-metals.
rubric.description: Compare lustre.
rubric.how: State that metals are generally lustrous and non-metals generally dull.

rubric.why: Physical shaping properties are characteristic of metals.
rubric.description: Compare malleability or ductility.
rubric.how: State that metals are malleable or ductile and contrast non-metals as brittle.

rubric.why: Conductivity is a key distinguishing property.
rubric.description: Compare electrical or thermal conductivity.
rubric.how: State that metals conduct well and non-metals generally conduct poorly.

rubric.why: Physical state provides another valid comparison.
rubric.description: Compare the states of the elements.
rubric.how: Mention that nearly all metals are solids while non-metals can be gases or solids.

rubric.why: The final comparison point completes the response.
rubric.description: Compare melting points or give a complete comparison.
rubric.how: State that metals generally have higher melting points than non-metals.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous, while non-metals are generally dull.
Metals are malleable and ductile, while solid non-metals are usually brittle.
Metals conduct heat and electricity well; non-metals are generally poor conductors.
Almost all metals are solids, while non-metals may be gases or solids.
Metals generally have higher melting points than non-metals.

written.text: Q9.7. V₂O₅ catalyst is preferred over platinum in the oxidation of sulphur dioxide. Give reasons.
written.finalAnswer: V₂O₅ is preferred because it is less expensive than platinum and is less easily poisoned by impurities while effectively catalysing the oxidation of sulphur dioxide.

rubric.why: The preferred catalyst must be identified.
rubric.description: Name V₂O₅ as the preferred catalyst.
rubric.how: Give its formula or name.

rubric.why: Cost is an important reason for choosing the catalyst.
rubric.description: Compare its cost with platinum.
rubric.how: State that V₂O₅ is cheaper.

rubric.why: Resistance to poisoning helps the catalyst keep working.
rubric.description: Compare how readily impurities poison it.
rubric.how: State that V₂O₅ is less easily poisoned by impurities.

rubric.why: The answer must connect the catalyst to the reaction in the question.
rubric.description: Identify the oxidation catalysed.
rubric.how: State that it catalyses the conversion of sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide.

modelAnswer: V₂O₅ is used as the catalyst for the oxidation of sulphur dioxide.
It is less expensive than platinum.
It is less easily poisoned by impurities.
It effectively catalyses the oxidation of sulphur dioxide to sulphur trioxide.

written.text: Q9.1. Explain the role of sodium as heat transfer agent in the atomic nuclear power plant. Which property of sodium is utilized in this role?
written.finalAnswer: Liquid sodium carries heat from the nuclear reactor core to the steam-generating system. Its high thermal conductivity is utilized.

rubric.why: The material's role must be identified.
rubric.description: State that sodium acts as the heat-transfer agent.
rubric.how: Name sodium as the coolant or heat-transfer material.

rubric.why: The answer must state where sodium receives heat.
rubric.description: Identify the heat source.
rubric.how: Mention the reactor core.

rubric.why: This describes where the transported heat is used.
rubric.description: Explain that sodium carries heat to the steam-producing system.
rubric.how: State that the heat is transferred to water or a steam generator.

rubric.why: The question specifically asks which property is used.
rubric.description: Name the property utilized.
rubric.how: State that sodium has high thermal conductivity.

modelAnswer: Liquid sodium absorbs heat from the reactor core.
It carries this heat to the steam-generating system.
The heat is used to produce steam.
Sodium's high thermal conductivity is utilized.

written.text: Q9.2. Why and how does lithium behave differently from the rest of the alkali metals?
written.finalAnswer: Lithium behaves differently because its atoms and Li⁺ ions are very small and have high charge density. It forms some more covalent compounds, reacts with nitrogen to form lithium nitride, and shows a diagonal relationship with magnesium.

rubric.why: The answer must identify lithium's unusual behaviour.
rubric.description: State that lithium behaves differently from the other alkali metals.
rubric.how: Describe it as showing anomalous behaviour.

rubric.why: Lithium's small size is the main cause of its distinctive behaviour.
rubric.description: Give the size reason.
rubric.how: State that lithium atoms or Li⁺ ions are unusually small.

rubric.why: High charge density explains why lithium compounds can differ in bonding.
rubric.description: Explain the effect of its small ion.
rubric.how: Mention high charge density or polarising power.

rubric.why: A distinctive compound or bonding property demonstrates how lithium behaves differently.
rubric.description: Give one example of lithium's unusual chemistry.
rubric.how: Mention more covalent compounds or its reaction with nitrogen to form Li₃N.

rubric.why: The diagonal relationship is another important comparison for lithium.
rubric.description: State lithium's relationship with magnesium.
rubric.how: Explain that lithium shows similarities to magnesium.

modelAnswer: Lithium behaves differently from the other alkali metals because its atoms and Li⁺ ions are very small.
The small Li⁺ ion has high charge density and high polarising power.
Lithium forms some compounds with greater covalent character.
It also reacts with nitrogen to form lithium nitride, Li₃N.
Lithium shows a diagonal relationship with magnesium.

written.text: Q9.3. Why aluminum metal is used in the manufacture of cooking utensils whereas magnesium is not considered useful for this purpose?
written.finalAnswer: Aluminium is a good conductor of heat, is light and forms a protective oxide layer. Magnesium is more reactive and can burn readily, so it is less suitable for cooking utensils.

rubric.why: Heat conduction is important for a cooking utensil.
rubric.description: State that aluminium conducts heat well.
rubric.how: Connect its thermal conductivity to cooking.

rubric.why: These properties make aluminium practical and durable.
rubric.description: Give another useful property of aluminium.
rubric.how: Mention low mass or its protective oxide layer.

rubric.why: Magnesium's reactivity is a reason it is less suitable.
rubric.description: State a drawback of magnesium.
rubric.how: Explain that it is reactive or can burn readily.

rubric.why: The answer must clearly compare the metals for the stated use.
rubric.description: Conclude why magnesium is not preferred.
rubric.how: Link its reactivity or burning risk to its unsuitability.

modelAnswer: Aluminium conducts heat well, so it is useful for cooking utensils.
It is light and its protective oxide layer helps prevent further corrosion.
Magnesium is more reactive and can burn readily.
Therefore, magnesium is less suitable for making cooking utensils.

examTips: Short questions often ask for a group trend, a reason for a physical state, or the role of an element in a reaction; give the fact and the reason.
Constructed-response questions commonly compare two groups or elements. State both sides of the comparison rather than describing only one.
For displacement and redox questions, identify which species loses or gains electrons and use the balanced reaction as evidence.
For descriptive answers, earn marks by linking a property to its effect: for example, a weaker bond breaks more easily on heating.
When a question asks for reasons, number or separate each reason clearly so the examiner can award each marking point.

steps.why: This identifies the trend that must be explained.
steps.text: Down Group 1, the atomic size of the alkali metals increases.

steps.why: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded.
steps.text: The outer electron is held less strongly by the nucleus.

steps.why: An electron that is held less strongly is removed more easily in a reaction.
steps.text: The outer electron is lost more easily.

steps.why: Losing the outer electron is how an alkali metal reacts.
steps.text: Therefore, the reactivity of alkali metals increases down the group.

example.question: Q9.1. Why does it become easier to cut an alkali metal when we move from top to bottom in a group?
example.answer: Metallic bonding becomes weaker down the group, so the alkali metals become softer and easier to cut.

explain.title: Alkali metals
explain.body: Alkali metals have one outer electron and readily lose it to form positive ions. Their reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron becomes easier to remove. They are generally soft metals with low melting points.

explain.title: Halogens
explain.body: Halogens gain one electron to form negative ions. Their reactivity decreases down the group because the atoms become larger and attract an incoming electron less strongly. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from its salt.

explain.title: Metallic and non-metallic properties
explain.body: Strong metallic bonding makes metals generally strong, malleable and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals do not have this metallic bonding and may be gases or brittle solids.

explain.title: Transition elements and catalysts
explain.body: Transition elements show distinctive properties such as variable oxidation states, coloured compounds and catalytic activity. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

explain.title: Noble gases and physical states
explain.body: Noble gases are monoatomic and unreactive. Weak attractions between their atoms give them low boiling points. Halogen molecules become larger down the group, so their attractions increase and their physical states change from gases to liquid to solid.

mistakes: Do not reverse the trends: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group, while halogen reactivity decreases down the group.
Do not say that chlorine is less reactive than bromine; chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent.
In a redox question, distinguish the oxidising agent from the reducing agent: the oxidising agent gains electrons, while the reducing agent loses electrons.
Do not give a trend without its reason when the question asks “why”; link it to electron loss, electron gain, atomic size or bond strength.
When describing a catalyst, explain how it helps the reaction rather than saying it is used up.
